fact_text: Commonly believed: the Norwegian employer's payroll office or NAV issues the A1 portable document because Denis is on the Norwegian payroll. Actually: the A1 certificate (which proves which country's social-security legislation applies and protects against double contribution demands) is issued by the competent institution of the Member State whose legislation applies. Because France is the competent state under Art. 11(3)(a), the A1 is issued by URSSAF on behalf of France. Action required: apply to URSSAF for the A1 certificate confirming French legislation; present to the Norwegian employer to cease Norwegian contributions.

fact_text: Art. 11(3)(a) applies so long as Denis's employed activity is exclusively or predominantly in France. If he subsequently performs 25% or more of his working time or earnings in Norway, Regulation 883/2004 Art. 13(1) replaces Art. 11 and requires a new determination: (a) legislation of the residence state (France) if substantial activity is performed there, or (b) legislation of the employer's registered office state (Norway) if no substantial activity occurs in the residence state. The 25% threshold is assessed over a representative reference period. Action required: Denis should track work-location split; any material shift toward Norwegian territory requires a new A1 determination from the competent institution.

fact_text: Under Regulation 883/2004 Art. 11(1), only one Member State's legislation applies at a time. Once French legislation is determined as applicable under Art. 11(3)(a), Denis is no longer covered by Norwegian mandatory social insurance. Mandatory membership in Norwegian national insurance (folketrygdloven §2-14) ceases when a person takes up residence abroad with the intention that the stay will last longer than 12 months. Because Denis relocates permanently to France, Norwegian mandatory coverage ends upon transfer. Voluntary continuation of Norwegian coverage (§2-7) may be elected separately but is not automatic.

fact_text: Commonly believed: because Denis is paid by a Norwegian employer on a Norwegian payroll, Norwegian social-security law (folketrygden) continues to apply even when he works from France. Actually: under Regulation (EC) 883/2004 Art. 11(3)(a), a person pursuing an employed activity in a Member State is subject to the legislation of that Member State, regardless of the employer's location or the employee's residence. Because Denis performs his work in France, French social-security legislation is applicable from day one of French-based work. Action required: Denis and his employer must act on the basis that French — not Norwegian — contributions are owed from the commencement of work in France.

fact_text: Commonly believed: all foreign nationals working in Norway hold a D-number (temporary identifier), so a D-number closure step must be completed when leaving Norway. Actually: Denis is a French national who has resided and worked in Norway long enough to have been assigned a permanent fodselsnummer (11-digit Norwegian national identity number) rather than a temporary D-number. A fodselsnummer is a lifetime identifier; it is not closed or surrendered upon departure. The D-number closure procedure is categorically inapplicable to Denis. Action required: none regarding the identity number itself. Denis retains his fodselsnummer for life; it will continue to be used in Norwegian tax filings and any future Norwegian interactions.

fact_text: Regulation 987/2009 Art. 21(2) permits the employer and employee to agree that the employee will fulfil the employer's contribution-payment obligations on the employer's behalf, provided the employer notifies the competent institution. Whether URSSAF SFE accepts such a delegation arrangement for a full-time remote employee on a permanent basis (rather than a short posting), the precise form of the delegation agreement, SFE's account-opening procedure, and the timeline for onboarding the Norwegian employer are unresolved practice-level questions. The regulatory right exists; its operational acceptance by SFE in this specific fact pattern requires confirmation from SFE directly or from a French social-law practitioner.

fact_text: Commonly believed: a Norwegian employer with no office or subsidiary in France has no French legal obligation when an employee simply works remotely from France. Actually: under Regulation 987/2009 Art. 21(1), an employer situated outside the competent Member State must fulfil all obligations laid down by the applicable legislation — including paying contributions — as if it had its registered office in the competent Member State (France). In practice this means the Norwegian employer must register with URSSAF's Service Firmes Etrangeres (SFE), the dedicated unit handling foreign firms. Failure to register and pay French employer contributions is a breach of French social law regardless of the employer's seat in Norway. Action required: the Norwegian employer must contact URSSAF SFE to open an account and begin French payroll filings.

fact_text: The France-Norway income and capital tax convention (signed 19 December 1980) contains an Art. 15 on income from employment. The standard OECD-model rule allocates taxation to the residence state (France) unless: (a) the employee is present in the source state (Norway) for more than 183 days in a 12-month period, or (b) the remuneration is paid by or on behalf of an employer resident in the source state AND (c) the remuneration is borne by a permanent establishment of the employer in the source state. Whether Denis's Norwegian employer's payroll constitutes remuneration 'borne by' a Norwegian establishment, how the 183-day count runs during the transition window, and whether France applies the credit or exemption method to avoid double taxation of any Norwegian-source portion, are unresolved questions that turn on the precise treaty text and current administrative practice. French and Norwegian tax counsel must advise.

fact_text: CGI Art. 4 B establishes four alternative criteria for French tax domicile; satisfying any one is sufficient: (1) foyer — habitual household residence in France; (2) principal place of abode — spending at least 183 days in France during the calendar year; (3) principal professional activity — the activity that consumes the most effective working time or generates the primary income is performed in France; (4) centre of economic interests — principal investments, business seat, or asset management are in France. For Denis, criteria (1) and (3) are both met from day one of his return: his foyer returns to France and his professional activity (remote work for the Norwegian employer) is physically performed in France. Multiple criteria being met simultaneously reinforces the residency determination.

fact_text: Commonly believed: Denis may retain Norwegian tax residency because he is paid by a Norwegian employer and his employment contract is governed by Norwegian law. Actually: under CGI Art. 4 B, a person whose foyer — defined as the habitual residence of the household — is located in France is a French tax resident, regardless of the nationality of the employer or the currency of payment. French tax residency triggers liability on worldwide income under CGI Art. 4 A. Denis's return to France with his household meets the foyer criterion immediately upon arrival. Action required: Denis must file French tax returns declaring worldwide income from the first year of return; he should also notify Skatteetaten of changed tax residency (handled separately in the origin-side batch).

fact_text: Denis simultaneously (a) resides in France and (b) works in France for a Norwegian employer whose French social-security registration (URSSAF SFE) may not be immediate. Whether worker-affiliation automatically pre-empts PUMa, whether PUMa fills the gap during employer-registration latency, and what documentation the local CPAM requires in the interim, are unresolved practice questions that depend on the actual registration timeline and local CPAM practice.

fact_text: Two distinct legal pathways govern CPAM affiliation for a person in Denis's position. Route 1 — Worker-affiliation: salaried workers covered by French social security are affiliated to the general health insurance scheme immediately upon commencement of employment activity in France; no waiting period applies for occupational coverage. Route 2 — PUMa (protection universelle maladie): under the universal health protection regime, any person residing in France on a stable and regular basis is entitled to health coverage; however, the 'stable and regular' residence criterion is typically satisfied after approximately 3 months of actual residence, and individuals relying solely on PUMa must file a Cerfa S1106 form with their local CPAM. The fact that both routes exist is assertable; which route governs on day one is a counsel question.

fact_text: Commonly believed: holding a Norwegian passport alongside a French passport may create a separate immigration obligation or ambiguity when returning to France. Actually: under Directive 2004/38/EC Art. 3(1) the Directive applies to Union citizens moving to a Member State 'other than that of which they are a national.' A French national returning to France is exercising rights under French domestic law and EU citizenship, not the Directive. The engine resolves nationality to FR (destination's own nationality takes priority over other EU/EEA or third-country nationalities). The outcome is nothing_to_do: 'French national exercising free movement; NO and SE nationalities are redundant for French immigration purposes.' The Norwegian nationality never disadvantages Denis; social-security analysis is nationality-agnostic. Action required: no immigration filing of any kind.

fact_text: Under Norwegian domestic tax law (skatteloven), once Denis ceases to be a Norwegian tax resident (after the Skatteloven §2-1(3) 3-year look-back period — covered in the origin-side batch), Norway retains limited source-taxation rights over Norwegian-source income. The open question is whether income paid by a Norwegian employer for remote work physically performed in France constitutes Norwegian-source income subject to Norwegian withholding (kildeskatt), or whether the physical performance of work in France breaks the Norwegian source nexus entirely. Norwegian domestic law and any treaty override under the FR-NO convention Art. 15 must both be analysed. Norwegian PAYE withholding practice for outbound remote workers and any one-year transition rule add further uncertainty. Norwegian and French tax counsel should confirm whether Norwegian PAYE withholding should cease immediately or continue during a transition period.
